_meta.purpose: STOF Session Management Weakness Knowledge Base -- real disclosed bug bounty patterns for stof/modules/session_weakness_tests.py.
sources: HackerOne #135797, #6504, #1486341 (Enter/ReddAPI/Acronis) -- session ID not regenerated on login
HackerOne #2582 (Slack) -- session fixation via session ID embedded in URL, persisting indefinitely
HackerOne #1162443 (Shopify), #193556 (Gratipay), #737058 (Clario) -- session/token remains valid after logout

HackerOne 'Breaking the Competition' writeup -- session tokens remain valid even after the user changes/resets their password; logout of one session cannot be forced by the victim on an attacker's stolen session

HackerOne #727487 (Snapchat), #1011767 (Yelp), #225897 (Dashlane), #723974 (Moneybird), #855013/#1076047 (Stripo), #1067533/#1206777 (Courier) -- rate limit/lockout bypass via a spoofed X-Forwarded-For header accepted at face value

HackerOne's own 2020 incident report (TechTarget/SC Media coverage) -- a session cookie not bound to any device/location was usable from a different machine entirely; HackerOne's own remediation was to bind sessions to the sign-in IP. HackerOne #19640, #1201396 (UPchieve) -- session hijacking via an unbound session token
Bugcrowd disclosure a655d2f1 (exposed API endpoints leading to user info disclosure) -- an authenticated API surface with no rate limiting at all, distinct from and beyond login-only throttling
_meta.key_finding: STOF already covers the two most commonly disclosed patterns directly: TC-129.1 (session ID not regenerated on login) and TC-129.2 (session valid after logout -- already LIVE-CONFIRMED FAILING on this project's own real target this session). Password-change session invalidation (TC-129.4) and session/auth cookie security-flag analysis (TC-129.5, LIVE-CONFIRMED FAILING against demo.testfire.net's missing-HttpOnly 'AltoroAccounts' cookie) close the two most recently identified gaps.
cookie_security_flags_sources: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet -- HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite attribute guidance for session cookies
HackerOne #5204 (Coinbase), #239380 (Stellar.org), #7033 (IRCCloud) -- session cookie missing the HttpOnly flag
HackerOne #343928 -- session cookie missing the Secure flag
session_timeout_concurrent_entropy_sourc: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet, 'Session Expiration' section -- idle timeout (2-30 min depending on risk) and absolute timeout (4-8h for typical full-day usage) guidance; fetched and read directly for this wave (2026-08-27), not from memory

OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet, 'Session ID Properties'/'Renew the Session ID After Any Privilege Level Change' sections -- concurrent-session revocation-on-login guidance: applications that disallow simultaneous logins should actively terminate the prior session when a new authentication event occurs
OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet, 'Session ID Entropy' -- session identifiers must carry at least 64 bits of entropy generated by a CSPRNG, with no fixed/predictable/sequential component

Bugcrowd disclosure 'Old session does not expire after setup 2FA' (CrowdStream) and Bugcrowd disclosure 'Failure to Invalid Session after Password Change' -- concurrent/stale session persistence after a re-authentication-shaped event

HackerOne #514577 (Omise) 'Failure to Invalid Session after...' and HackerOne #1118402/#678050 (Liberapay) -- session not invalidated on a subsequent authentication event, the same family this wave's concurrent-session technique targets

Cobalt.io Pentest Vulnerability Wiki, 'Session Token Predictable' -- disclosed pattern: sequencer-style comparison of tokens issued across independent logins to detect shared prefixes, sequential/incrementing numeric identifiers, or low character-set variety

stof_coverage.status: covered, live-confirmed vulnerable on real target

patterns.generalized_transformation: Capture a session's cookie value, trigger a password change/reset through that same session, then replay the ORIGINAL (pre-change) cookie against a protected page. Real reports show this frequently succeeds even when logout invalidation works correctly -- password change is a distinct code path that developers often forget carries the same 'kill every other session' obligation.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: POST to the discovered change-password endpoint, followed by a GET to a known authenticated-only page using the pre-change cookie.
patterns.real_example: 'Breaking the Competition' (HackerOne): even after the user changes or resets their password, ALL previously-issued sessions remain valid -- the victim has no way to force-invalidate a stolen session short of that exact session's own logout.
patterns.evidence_signal: The pre-change cookie still authenticates successfully (still-200/authenticated response) on a protected page after the password change completes.

stof_coverage.note: Implemented in stof/modules/session_weakness_tests.py, same plant/verify shape as TC-129.2 (capture cookie -> trigger event -> replay old cookie), triggered by a real password-change request instead of a logout. Gated behind AuthTestConfig.allow_state_changing_probes (off by default); reverts the password back to its original value afterward. Live-validated against demo.testfire.net this session: correctly SKIPPED (no change_password_url configured for that target), same gating behavior as the sibling password-change techniques TC-025.1-5/TC-027.4.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Capture the anonymous pre-login cookie jar, force a real fresh login, capture the post-login cookie jar, and keep only the cookies that are NEW or have a CHANGED value across that boundary -- the same diffing primitive TC-129.1 already uses, just kept as raw cookie objects (not collapsed to name:value) since the flags being checked live there. For each such cookie, check (in priority order): HttpOnly missing (highest-confidence signal), Secure missing (only on an https:// target), and SameSite=None set without Secure. SameSite missing entirely is deliberately NOT a finding -- modern browsers already default it to Lax.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any target with a real login flow: an anonymous GET followed by a forced fresh authentication for the configured test role, both against the same target URL used elsewhere in TC-129 (login_json_endpoint / change_password_url / first discovered endpoint).
patterns.evidence_signal: A session/auth cookie -- identified purely by the new-or-changed diff, never by name-pattern guessing -- carries `httpOnly: false`, or `secure: false` on an https:// target, or `sameSite: 'None'` without `secure: true`.
patterns.real_example: HackerOne #5204 (Coinbase), #239380 (Stellar.org), #7033 (IRCCloud): session cookie missing HttpOnly, allowing theft via any XSS on the page. HackerOne #343928: session cookie missing Secure, allowing interception over a downgraded/mixed-content connection.

stof_coverage.note: Implemented in stof/modules/session_weakness_tests.py as _technique_cookie_security_flags, reusing _force_fresh_login exactly like TC-129.1. Two pure, directly-unit-tested helpers: _new_or_changed_cookies(anon_cookies, authenticated_cookies) -> dict[str, dict] (the new-or-changed diff, kept as full Playwright cookie objects) and _cookie_flag_issue(cookie, is_https_target) -> str | None (HttpOnly checked first, then Secure gated on an https:// target, then SameSite=None-without-Secure; SameSite simply absent is never checked at all, so it can never be flagged). FAILs on the first real issue found across the identified session/auth cookies, PASSes when all of them carry correct flags, SKIPs when no cookie was new-or-changed across the login boundary (e.g. a non-cookie-based auth target). Live-validated against demo.testfire.net (2026-08-27, scan_45f2c657): result FAIL, live-confirmed -- role 'normal's 'AltoroAccounts' cookie was newly issued at login (present in the post-login jar, absent from the anonymous pre-login jar) and is missing the HttpOnly flag, exactly the highest-confidence, first-priority check per the research. allow_state_changing_probes remained false/untouched for this run (this technique never gates on it).

patterns.generalized_transformation: Session identifier embedded in the URL itself (not a cookie) persists indefinitely and leaks via Referer headers, browser history, and server logs.
patterns.real_example: Slack (HackerOne #2582): a valid session-bearing URL remained active indefinitely.

stof_coverage.gap: STOF's session model assumes cookie-based sessions throughout (Session.cookies). A URL-embedded session identifier is a distinct, less common pattern in modern apps (mostly legacy/JSP-era, ironically including this project's own demo.testfire.net target which does use JSESSIONID in some contexts) -- noted as a real but lower-priority gap, not built this wave.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Actually waiting out a real idle/absolute timeout window live inside an automated scan is impractical (OWASP's own guidance ranges from a 2-minute idle timeout up to an 8-hour absolute timeout -- no bounded scan can honestly wait that out without becoming a multi-hour, mostly-idle process). Instead: force a real fresh login for the configured test role and inspect the resulting Session's own `expires_at` field, which STOF's Session model (stof/session/models.py) already carries when the target exposes any expiry signal (a JWT `exp` claim, a Set-Cookie `Max-Age`/`Expires`, or a token endpoint's own expiry field) -- this is a structural/observational check ('is any expiry information observable at all, and if so is it consistent with a bounded absolute timeout'), never a fabricated live-wait test.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: A real fresh authentication for the configured test role, comparing the resulting Session.expires_at against Session.created_at -- no HTTP probe beyond the login itself.
patterns.evidence_signal: SKIPPED when Session.expires_at is None (no expiry information observable on this session for this target/auth_type -- honest 'cannot test this live' outcome, not a false negative). FAIL when expires_at IS observable but the created_at-to-expires_at span exceeds 24 hours (a generous multiple over OWASP's own ~4-8h absolute-timeout guidance, chosen specifically to avoid flagging legitimate longer-lived tokens as a false positive). PASS when an observable expiry falls within that bound.
patterns.real_example: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet's own 'Session Expiration' section: idle timeout 2-30 minutes depending on application risk, absolute timeout typically 4-8 hours for a full working-day usage pattern -- sessions with no enforced expiration at all are a recurring real-world session-management weakness this cheat sheet exists specifically to warn against.

stof_coverage.status: covered (structural/observational check, honestly scoped -- see technique docstring)
stof_coverage.note: Implemented in stof/modules/session_weakness_tests.py as _technique_session_timeout, reusing _force_fresh_login exactly like TC-129.1/TC-129.5. Pure helper _session_timeout_issue(created_at, expires_at) -> str | None does the 24h-threshold comparison and is directly unit-tested. Deliberately legitimately SKIPs (not a fabricated PASS/FAIL) whenever the target's Session carries no expires_at at all -- e.g. cookie-only auth with no JWT exp/Max-Age STOF observes -- since there is no honest non-destructive way to test real timeout behavior live in a bounded scan for that case. Live-validated against demo.testfire.net (2026-08-27, scan_fe590f76): result SKIPPED, live-confirmed -- role 'normal's form_login Session carried no expires_at (demo.testfire.net's own JSESSIONID/AltoroAccounts cookies expose no JWT exp claim or comparable expiry STOF could read), the honest by-design outcome, not a fabricated timing test.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Authenticate twice, live, for the same configured test role (two real logins through the existing form_login/jwt flow, each producing its own cookie jar via SessionManager.invalidate()+authenticate() -- the exact same _force_fresh_login mechanism TC-129.1/.2/.4/.5 already use, called twice instead of once). After the second login completes, replay the FIRST session's captured cookies against a known authenticated page/endpoint. If that first session still authenticates, the target does not revoke prior sessions when a new one is established for the same account -- the same 'plant a cookie, trigger a re-auth-shaped event, replay the old cookie' shape as TC-129.2 (logout) and TC-129.4 (password change), just triggered by a second real login instead.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Two real logins for the same role against the target's own login flow, followed by a GET replay of the first session's cookies against a discovered endpoint or the login page itself.
patterns.evidence_signal: The first session's cookie jar still returns an ALLOWED-classified response (via authorization.decision.classify_response, same oracle as TC-129.2/.4) after a second, independent login for the same role has completed.
patterns.real_example: Bugcrowd 'Old session does not expire after setup 2FA' and 'Failure to Invalid Session after Password Change'; HackerOne #514577 (Omise), #1118402/#678050 (Liberapay) -- all disclosed reports in the same 'a subsequent authentication-shaped event for the account should revoke prior sessions, and frequently doesn't' family. OWASP's Session Management Cheat Sheet explicitly recommends actively terminating a prior session when a new one is established, for applications that intend to disallow concurrent logins.

stof_coverage.status: covered, live-confirmed vulnerable on real target
stof_coverage.note: Implemented in stof/modules/session_weakness_tests.py as _technique_concurrent_session_not_revoked. No new payload or gating: two calls to the existing _force_fresh_login, then the same cookie-replay-and-classify pattern TC-129.2/.4 already use. Never gated behind allow_state_changing_probes -- a second real login is the same non-destructive class of action as every other technique in this module (unlike TC-129.4's real password change). A transient probe failure on the replay surfaces as ERROR, never a silent PASS, matching this module's existing transient-error convention. Live-validated against demo.testfire.net (2026-08-27, scan_fe590f76): result FAIL, live-confirmed -- role 'normal's first-login session cookie still authenticated (HTTP 200) against the target after a second, independent login for the same role completed, meaning demo.testfire.net does not revoke prior sessions on a subsequent login.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Capture the SAME-named session/auth cookie's value across two independent fresh logins for the same test role (again via _force_fresh_login, called twice -- the same mechanism TC-129.7 uses). Purely observational analysis of the two captured values (never brute-forcing or guessing another user's token): flag a short token (<16 chars), a long shared prefix between the two independently-issued values (>=50% of the shorter value's length and >=8 chars), two purely-numeric values differing by a small integer (a sequential/incrementing identifier), or a value using 4 or fewer distinct characters. Two identical values across logins is deliberately NOT flagged here -- that is TC-129.1's session-fixation-on-rotation-failure finding, not an entropy finding, and double-reporting the same root cause under two vuln_types would be noise.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Two real logins for the same role, comparing the value of whichever cookie name is present in both resulting cookie jars.
patterns.evidence_signal: Any of: token length under 16 characters; a shared prefix across two independent logins covering at least half the shorter token's length; two purely-numeric tokens whose difference is under 1000; a token using 4 or fewer distinct characters. A legitimately random-looking token (long, high character variety, no shared prefix, non-numeric or a numeric value differing by a large/non-sequential amount) must NOT trigger any of these -- verified directly in unit tests as a false-positive guard.
patterns.real_example: Cobalt.io Pentest Vulnerability Wiki 'Session Token Predictable' entry describes exactly this sequencer-style technique: comparing tokens issued across independent sessions for shared structure, sequential values, or embedded predictable components, the same class of finding OWASP's Session Management Cheat Sheet's 64-bit-entropy/CSPRNG requirement exists to prevent.

stof_coverage.status: covered, live-confirmed on real target (no low-entropy pattern found)
stof_coverage.note: Implemented in stof/modules/session_weakness_tests.py as _technique_session_token_entropy. Pure, directly-unit-tested helper _token_entropy_issue(value_a, value_b) -> str | None does the length/prefix/sequential-numeric/charset checks and is exercised against both positive cases and an explicit false-positive guard case (a long, high-variety, non-matching-prefix token pair must return None). Never attempts to guess or brute-force another user's session -- both values it compares are captured from the module's OWN two fresh logins for the configured test role. Live-validated against demo.testfire.net (2026-08-27, scan_fe590f76): result PASS, live-confirmed -- the shared session cookie(s) captured across two independent logins for role 'normal' showed no shared-prefix/sequential-numeric/short-length/low-charset pattern.

patterns.generalized_transformation: After a real login-rate-limit/lockout signal has already been observed (reusing TC-129.3's own bounded attempt loop and lockout-signal classifier), send ONE more identical wrong-credential attempt with a spoofed X-Forwarded-For and X-Real-IP header claiming a different, non-routable (RFC 5737 TEST-NET-3) source IP. If that follow-up attempt is accepted without the same challenge, the lockout is keyed off an attacker-controlled header rather than (or in addition to) the real connecting IP or account identifier. Never sends more than the original bounded attempt count plus one extra probe -- this is a bypass check for a lockout that already fired, not a second brute-force run.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any login endpoint (JSON API or discovered HTML form) that TC-129.3 already established DOES enforce some rate-limiting/lockout signal (HTTP 429, or a CAPTCHA/lockout-shaped response body).
patterns.evidence_signal: The spoofed-header follow-up attempt returns neither HTTP 429 nor a CAPTCHA/lockout-shaped body, immediately after the same request shape (without the spoofed header) had triggered exactly that signal.
patterns.real_example: Six independently disclosed HackerOne reports (Snapchat #727487, Yelp #1011767, Dashlane #225897, Moneybird #723974, Stripo #855013/#1076047, Courier #1067533/#1206777) all describe the identical bypass: a rate-limited/throttled endpoint stopped enforcing its limit the moment the attacker varied the X-Forwarded-For header per request, because the server trusted the client-supplied header as the real source IP.

stof_coverage.note: Implemented in stof/modules/session_weakness_tests.py as _technique_lockout_bypass_via_xff. SKIPs honestly (rather than false-PASS/FAIL) when TC-129.3's own loop never observes a lockout signal in the first place -- there is nothing to test bypassing. Reuses classify_response()'s existing CHALLENGED mapping and _LOCKOUT_SIGNAL_MARKERS, same as TC-129.3.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Reuses TC-129.3's exact bounded-attempt-count / lockout-signal-classification shape, but retargets it at a discovered, authenticated GET API endpoint (using the configured test role's real session) instead of the unauthenticated login endpoint -- checking whether rate limiting exists ANYWHERE beyond the login form, which is the far more commonly protected surface.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any discovered endpoint_type=='api', method=='GET' endpoint, called repeatedly with a real authenticated session.
patterns.evidence_signal: No HTTP 429 or throttling-shaped response across the same bounded attempt count TC-129.3 uses, while authenticated.
patterns.real_example: Bugcrowd disclosure a655d2f1: an authenticated API endpoint disclosing user information had no rate limiting at all, permitting unbounded enumeration -- the exact 'protected the login form, forgot everything behind it' pattern this technique targets.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Force a real fresh login, capture the resulting session cookie(s), then replay those exact cookies in a brand-new anonymous browser context whose User-Agent header is deliberately set to a completely different device/browser/OS (a Chrome-on-Android UA replacing whatever logged in). If the replayed session is still accepted, nothing about the session ties it to the client that created it -- a stolen cookie alone (no other client secret) is sufficient to fully hijack the session from an unrelated device.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any authenticated GET endpoint, probed first with the real session/role, then replayed with the same cookies under a spoofed User-Agent via a fresh anonymous context.
patterns.evidence_signal: The replayed request under a different User-Agent still returns an authenticated (ALLOWED) response.
patterns.real_example: HackerOne's own disclosed 2020 incident: a support session cookie was not bound to any device or location, and was accepted from an entirely different machine than the one that created it -- rated Critical, paid a $20,000 bounty, and HackerOne's own remediation was binding sessions to the sign-in IP. HackerOne #1201396 (UPchieve) independently describes the same unbound-session-hijacking root cause.

stof_coverage.note: Implemented in stof/modules/session_weakness_tests.py as _technique_session_not_bound_to_client. Framed as Low severity / defense-in-depth in the Finding description -- per-request client-fingerprint binding has real usability tradeoffs and is unusual outside high-security contexts, so this is reported honestly as a hardening gap alongside session lifetime/rotation controls, never as a standalone required fix.
